g.text: Every overlap between two sorted lists — stack and heap at every step
3 vs 2 spans → 2 overlaps · 6 comparisons vs 4 · 1 of 3 droppable
1 // primitive: len(xs) — element count. len(LEFT) = 3 · len(RIGHT) = 2
2 // primitive: LEFT / RIGHT — two lists of spans, each sorted and none overlapping its
6 // primitive: startOf(x) / endOf(x) — the two ends of a span.
8 // primitive: maxOf(a, b) / minOf(a, b) — the larger and smaller of two numbers.
10 // primitive: span(lo, hi) — one overlap. span(1, 3) = 1..3
11 // primitive: NONE — these two spans do not overlap at all.
14 // "Two sorted lists of time spans. Within a list, spans never overlap each other.
15 // Report every overlap between a LEFT span and a RIGHT one. 10^6 spans each. Then:
16 // both lists are streams that keep arriving — what may you throw away?"
18 // function: overlapOf(x, y) — the overlap, or NONE. Two lines, and they are the only
19 // geometry in the problem: it starts at the later start and ends at the earlier end.
28 // function: everyPair(left, right) — the answer everyone gives first: try all of them.
41 // function: sweep(left, right) — one pointer into each list. After testing a pair,
42 // advance whichever span ENDS FIRST: it cannot overlap anything further along the
43 // other list, because that list is sorted and its spans only start later.
59 // function: droppable(left, bound) — spans that can be forgotten, because nothing still
60 // to arrive on the other side can start before `bound`.
70 // function: main() — every pair, then the sweep, then what may be discarded.
73 val fast = sweep(LEFT, RIGHT) // 4 comparisons, same 2 overlaps
0x100 holds 1..3 130..245 540..540 and 0x200 holds 50..150 220..320. Two facts are handed to you and both matter: each list is **sorted**, and within a list
the spans **never overlap each other**. The second is what makes the advance rule below sound, and it is easy to read past as scene-setting.

Step 2/0 — the overlap is two comparisons
130..245 and 50..150 overlap on 130..150: it starts at the **later** start and ends at the **earlier** end. If that comes out backwards — hi below lo — there is
no overlap, so one comparison answers both "do they" and "where". Getting this expression right first removes most of the fiddliness from the rest.

3 × 2 = 6 comparisons for 2 overlaps. Correct, and quadratic — at 10⁶ spans each that is 10¹² comparisons, so it is not slow, it is impossible. And the
sortedness has not been used at all.

Step 4/0 — the reframe: one pointer into each
Two cursors, both at the front. Because each list is sorted, everything after cursor `i` starts no earlier than `left[i]` — so the lists can be walked forward
once and never revisited. The only question is which cursor to move.

Step 5/0 — 1..3 ends before 50..150, so LEFT advances
**Advance whichever span ends first.** 1..3 ends at 3, before 50..150 ends at 150 — and every later RIGHT span starts after 50, so none of them can reach back to
3. 1..3 is finished with, permanently, and the non-overlapping guarantee is exactly what licenses that.

Step 6/0 — and here 50..150 ends first, so RIGHT advances
The rule is symmetric and must be, which is the part to get right: advancing the one that **starts** first, or always advancing left, skips overlaps. 130..245 is
still live and will be compared against the next RIGHT span — so a single LEFT span can produce several overlaps, and the loop does not assume one each.

Step 8/0 — a pair that does not overlap at all
1..3 and 50..150 give lo = 50 and hi = 3, so hi is below lo and there is nothing. The pair is still **compared**, which is the cost of the sweep: 4 comparisons,
one per advance, and some of them find nothing.

4 against 6 here — small lists, small margin. The shape is what matters: each comparison advances exactly one cursor, so the total is at most 3 + 2, and at 10⁶
spans each that is 2 × 10⁶ comparisons instead of 10¹². O(m+n) rather than O(mn), and no sorting needed because both inputs arrived sorted.

Step 10/0 — now the second half: both lists are streams
The sweep assumed both lists were complete. As streams they are not, and a LEFT span cannot be released the moment the cursor passes it — a RIGHT span that
overlaps it may not have arrived yet. So "finished with" becomes a claim about the **future**, which the sweep had no need to make.

Step 11/0 — 1 of 3 spans may be forgotten
Given a promise that nothing further from the RIGHT stream will start before 220, every LEFT span ending before 220 is safe to drop: 1..3. 130..245 and 540..540

Step 12/0 — so the bound is the whole design
Where does 220 come from? Not from the algorithm — from a declared limit on how far behind a stream may be, and it has to be the **minimum** over both sides,
because one silent stream means nothing can be released from either. That makes memory a function of the declared lateness bound rather than of the data, and it
means a stream that stops arriving stalls the join rather than breaking it. Naming that bound is the answer; the two-pointer sweep is the easy half.
